proposal.policy_prompt_for_action:
When reproducing the demonstrated planar stick route, the policy generally selected the correct chronological leg and correctly updated completed_legs, but placed bypass turns several centimetres beyond the demonstrated corner or placed gap arrivals short of or beyond their stopping point. The retained demonstration already contained the required history. These are action SUFFICIENCY failures in extracting metric endpoints, not failures of memory transitions. Strengthen the existing feature-identification and fitting rules with a concrete measurement-validation procedure rather than adding more route-history fields.

Before reconstructing endpoints, use the current calibrated TCP projection to identify the physical distal end of the rigid stick in the current front image. Compare the projected point with the visible end face and shaft boundaries, not just the lowest bright or gray pixel. Where the wrist image sees the tool, check the same physical identification there using its own calibration. Use this correspondence to establish which part of the rendered tool is the TCP. In demonstration frames, track that physical end face using the shaft's continuity and geometry; do not transfer a constant pixel displacement from the current image. A measurement on the marker, white trail, or silhouette edge below the end face must not enter the tip-height fit. If the end face cannot be distinguished, mark that measurement unavailable rather than reporting a precise coordinate from it.

Make endpoint reconstruction an explicit joint measurement problem. For each pending turn, identify its preceding arrival, incoming interior tip samples, outgoing interior tip samples, and following arrival. Record their chronological roles in the calculation before fitting. Fit a shared corner to both segments, permitting both world coordinates to vary. Project the resulting segments back into every usable supporting image and inspect residuals against the identified end-face centres. A candidate supported only by a shaft or trail feature, or by extending the incoming direction without agreement with outgoing observations, must be discarded. Sparse samples near a turn do not by themselves justify extra clearance or a longer leg. Where multiple feature interpretations are possible, compare their fits across the whole adjoining traversal rather than selecting each pixel independently. Retain the existing prohibition on converting elapsed control steps into constant-speed displacement.

For gap endpoints, jointly use all visits to that static gap, including a demonstrated starting or final position when available. Samples before an arrival and after its departure constrain different segments; neither is automatically the endpoint. In particular, a sample near the end of an approach must not become an early stopping point, and a subsequent departure sample must not extend the arrival. For final arrivals, validate the end-face identification against preceding frames before applying the ray-plane calculation. Reprojection checks arithmetic, not physical feature identity. If a route returns to its starting gap, use that retained starting view as an additional common-location constraint, without merging the visits in completed_legs.

Keep bypass coordinates specific to each chronological traversal: an outward and a return pass around the same obstacle can have different corners. Keep the existing full-endpoint commands, 0.07 m tip height, downward orientation, arrival tolerance, and count-update rules. Do not replace these with fixed offsets, nominal leg lengths, extra clearance, or episode-specific coordinate tables. No existing route-order rule needs removal; the change is to make validated physical-tip measurements and a jointly checked fit prerequisites for accepting its reconstructed endpoint.
proposal.refused: The reports repeatedly requested exact coordinates or particular frame-to-endpoint associations for individual bypasses and gaps. Those numerical targets are recorded answers, not additional history that a deployed policy can observe. They are not being passed on as lookup rules, color-specific routes, or new memory fields. The demonstration and completed-leg count were retained and used correctly throughout the reported failures, so neither a PREDICTABILITY defect nor an unused-memory NECESSITY defect was established. Many proposed remedies—fit both coordinates, intersect incoming and outgoing segments, preserve repeated visits, pool static-gap evidence, and avoid projecting ground markers onto the tip-height plane—were already explicit. Repeating them as separate clauses for each failed traversal would not resolve the shared measurement problem. The accepted correction instead makes physical feature validation and joint residual checking operational. Reports that supplied pixel/coordinate pairs are not accepted as authoritative calibration facts without independent verification. A current wrist view can validate the current tool feature but cannot reveal an unseen historical final wrist view. Failures that named no missing information are treated as additional localization errors, not evidence for a new memory transition or route rule.

policy_prompt_for_action.modify_from: At the initial act cycle, project the reported TCP into the current execution view to check which visible feature represents the free tip at z=0.07 m; do not transfer a constant image-space offset to other poses. For each usable demonstration frame, measure that same distal-tip feature, not the lowest pixel of the hand, the shaft centre, robot housing, marker or trail. An occluded distal end is an unavailable tip measurement, not permission to substitute a nearby feature.
policy_prompt_for_action.modify_to: Use the reported current TCP and front-camera calibration to check which physical feature represents the free tip at z=0.07 m. Compare its projection with the centre of the visible distal end face and the adjoining shaft boundaries, not merely the lowest bright or gray pixel. If the current wrist image shows the tool and its calibration is supplied, cross-check that same physical correspondence there. This validates the current feature identification, not an unseen historical wrist view. Track the corresponding distal end-face centre through demonstration frames using shaft continuity and geometry; do not transfer a constant image-space offset to other poses. Do not measure the lowest pixel of the hand, shaft centre, robot housing, marker, trail, or a silhouette edge below the end face. If the distal end face is occluded or cannot be distinguished reliably, treat its measurement as unavailable rather than assigning a precise coordinate to a substitute feature.

policy_prompt_for_action.modify_from: Project the recovered endpoint and both fitted segments back into the demonstration. Check that the assigned distal-tip observations lie on their respective segments in chronological order, that the endpoint follows the last incoming observation and precedes the first outgoing observation along the route, and that the demonstrated obstacle side is preserved. Reject an endpoint supported by extending only one fitted direction, misassigned arrival/departure evidence, or a rounded trail corner treated as a straight tip trajectory.
policy_prompt_for_action.modify_to: Validate the shared endpoint as a joint measurement fit: project it and both fitted segments into every usable supporting demonstration image and inspect residuals against the identified distal end-face centres, respecting measurement uncertainty. Keep each supporting observation assigned to its preceding arrival, incoming interior, outgoing interior, or following arrival role throughout the check. Where physical-feature interpretations are ambiguous, compare candidate interpretations jointly across the adjoining traversal rather than choosing each frame's pixel independently. Accept the fit only when reliable incoming and outgoing observations support their respective segments in chronological order, the endpoint follows the last incoming observation and precedes the first outgoing observation along the route, and the demonstrated obstacle side is preserved. Reject an endpoint supported only by shaft or trail features, by extending only one fitted direction, by misassigned arrival/departure evidence, or by a rounded trail corner treated as a straight tip trajectory. Numerical reprojection consistency alone does not validate physical feature identity.

revision.refused: No memory fields or transitions change: all reported memory values were correct, and no additional unavailable historical fact was identified. No episode-specific coordinates, frame-to-endpoint lookup clauses, fixed offsets, nominal lengths, extra clearance, or motion subdivisions are added. Existing joint fitting, static-gap evidence pooling, final-tip corroboration, chronological repetition, and height rules remain rather than being duplicated. No earlier edit is reverted: worse aggregate scores alone do not establish that an earlier rule caused the errors, and this report supplies no such evidence. The changes strengthen physical-feature validation and cross-frame residual checking without claiming that sparse or occluded observations always determine endpoints within one centimetre.

fields.name: demonstration
fields.description: At the video cycle, record the ordered list of all supplied demonstration frame labels, including the initial and final frames. Preserve this list unchanged throughout execution. These images specify the entire demonstrated route, including obstacle sides, intermediate turns, reversals, repeated visits and the stopping point; do not replace it with an unordered set of visited places. e.g. ["V0", "V16", "V32", "V48", "V64", "V80", "V96", "V99"]

These images specify the entire demonstrated route, including obstacle sides, intermediate turns, reversals, repeated visits and the stopping point; do not replace it with an unordered set of visited places. e.g. ["V0", "V16", "V32", "V48", "V64", "V80", "V96", "V99"]

fields.name: completed_legs
fields.description: Write zero at the video cycle and initial act cycle. At subsequent act cycles, use the incoming count to identify the next uncompleted endpoint in demonstration. Compare the current TCP and the observed motion with that endpoint. Increment by one only if the motion shown has reached it within 1 cm; otherwise preserve the count. Count bypass endpoints and repeated visits separately. An explicitly zero-step action, an incomplete approach or a wait does not advance the count. Record only arrivals already observed, never the endpoint of the action being selected now. e.g. 2
fields.annotation: The number of demonstrated waypoint-to-waypoint legs already completed by the execution at the current observation, excluding the action selected at this cycle. Set to zero at the video cycle and the initial act cycle. Increment when the observed execution reaches the next demonstrated leg endpoint within 1 cm. Count intermediate bypass points as endpoints, not just marked gaps. Repeated visits count separately in chronological order. Do not increment for a motion that executes no steps, an incomplete approach, or a wait. Preserve the count otherwise. e.g. 2

texts.action:
At the video cycle, produce memory only. At execution start, the stick is already at the demonstrated starting point: do not add a grasp, lift or approach action. Use demonstration to reconstruct the ordered planar route of the lower free end of the attached stick. Follow the actual stick tip, not the robot housing or the red marker: a red marker can remain at the previous gap while the tip travels around an obstacle. The white trail helps identify which side was traversed, but is not itself the complete task history.

Identify the ordered legs and assign demonstration frames to their incoming and outgoing segments, including bypasses beside obstacle ends and arrivals at gaps. Approximate 25-control-step boundaries are segmentation aids only: a nearby displayed frame need not show an endpoint, and elapsed time must not be converted into distance by assuming constant speed. Reconstruct unsampled endpoints geometrically as described below. Use the full video to distinguish retracing a bypass from continuing around the opposite end. Preserve all repetitions as separate chronological occurrences; reaching a previously visited gap does not mean the route is finished. Do not force bypass turns on opposite-direction traversals to share coordinates merely because they pass the same obstacle end. Do not assume that all obstacles must be visited or that every traversal alternates sides.

Identify the stick as the narrow rigid extension beneath the hand and track the centre of its distal end through the demonstration. Use the reported current TCP and front-camera calibration to check which physical feature represents the free tip at z=0.07 m. Compare its projection with the centre of the visible distal end face and the adjoining shaft boundaries, not merely the lowest bright or gray pixel. If the current wrist image shows the tool and its calibration is supplied, cross-check that same physical correspondence there. This validates the current feature identification, not an unseen historical wrist view. Track the corresponding distal end-face centre through demonstration frames using shaft continuity and geometry; do not transfer a constant image-space offset to other poses. Do not measure the lowest pixel of the hand, shaft centre, robot housing, marker, trail, or a silhouette edge below the end face. If the distal end face is occluded or cannot be distinguished reliably, treat its measurement as unavailable rather than assigning a precise coordinate to a substitute feature. Convert its pixel (u,v) into world coordinates using the camera calibration: C=-R^T t, d=R^T K^-1[u,v,1]^T, and X=C+((0.07-C_z)/d_z)d. Perform this ray-plane calculation rather than estimating metric offsets visually.

Before fitting an unsampled turn, assign each measurement to its chronological leg. Use the preceding arrival and samples strictly before the turn for the incoming segment, and samples strictly after the turn and the following arrival for the outgoing segment. Do not treat a departure sample as evidence of the preceding arrival. Fit the incoming and outgoing planar directions using multiple frames wherever available, preferentially using clear interior distal-tip measurements; downweight uncertain measurements and exclude occluded-tip substitutions. Fit both world x and y freely: an apparently axial image trajectory or vertical shaft does not justify preserving a current world coordinate. Extend both fitted segments to their intersection to recover the shared endpoint; with noisy observations, use a joint least-squares fit with a shared endpoint. Do not interpolate directly between the last incoming sample and first outgoing sample, which cuts across the corner. Those two samples alone do not determine two directions: use neighboring frames farther along each segment, clearly observed start or arrival positions, and obstacle geometry as additional constraints. For collinear reversals, where line intersection does not determine the endpoint, use observed arrival or repeated-visit evidence and gap geometry rather than inventing an intersection. Validate the shared endpoint as a joint measurement fit: project it and both fitted segments into every usable supporting demonstration image and inspect residuals against the identified distal end-face centres, respecting measurement uncertainty. Keep each supporting observation assigned to its preceding arrival, incoming interior, outgoing interior, or following arrival role throughout the check. Where physical-feature interpretations are ambiguous, compare candidate interpretations jointly across the adjoining traversal rather than choosing each frame's pixel independently. Accept the fit only when reliable incoming and outgoing observations support their respective segments in chronological order, the endpoint follows the last incoming observation and precedes the first outgoing observation along the route, and the demonstrated obstacle side is preserved. Reject an endpoint supported only by shaft or trail features, by extending only one fitted direction, by misassigned arrival/departure evidence, or by a rounded trail corner treated as a straight tip trajectory. Numerical reprojection consistency alone does not validate physical feature identity. If directions remain underconstrained, use adjoining arrival evidence and other demonstrated views of the same geometric location; do not invent a longer clearance move. When the tip is occluded, use neighboring visible tip positions, shaft and trail evidence, and obstacle geometry as supporting constraints; do not substitute shaft or trail pixels into the tip-height projection.

For a gap arrival, distinguish the full arrival from a sample still approaching the gap. Locate the endpoint from incoming and outgoing path evidence, refining it with the marked gap center only when the marker's own plane is established. Recover the marker's planar coordinates on that plane, then set the commanded TCP height to 0.07 m; never project a ground-marker pixel onto the tip-height plane. Gather arrival and departure evidence from all demonstrated visits to the same static gap to constrain its common location, including the retained starting view and any clear final visit. A still-approaching sample constrains the incoming segment, not the arrival position. Share the gap location without merging chronological occurrences: each visit consumes its own leg. Do not impose shared coordinates on bypass turns merely because they pass the same obstacle end. For the final endpoint, explicitly identify the distal-tip centre in the final demonstration frame and corroborate the feature identification with preceding arrival frames. Apply the calibrated z=0.07 m ray-plane calculation to that pixel and reproject the resulting coordinate to check numerical consistency; reprojection alone does not establish that the chosen feature is the tip. Discard any pixel/world-coordinate pair that disagrees under the calibration and resolve the measurement rather than accepting either as authoritative. If the final tip is occluded, use the existing occlusion and arrival-evidence rules, not a shaft or trail substitute. Do not extrapolate beyond the supported stopping point to a nominal gap coordinate or nominal leg length.

Use current front and wrist observations to refine alignment with the same static obstacle arrangement. Colors identify obstacles within the episode but do not define a universal route.

First evaluate whether the current observation completes the next leg, according to the completed_legs memory rule. With the resulting completed count c, command the endpoint of leg c+1. Set TCP z to 0.07 m and preserve the current approximately downward orientation, normalizing equivalent roll angles if needed. Keep the gripper closed; its command is ignored for this stick tool. Command the reconstructed absolute full leg endpoint, without coarse centimetre-scale rounding or added obstacle clearance. Neither a nominal leg length nor a fixed axial or diagonal offset defines that endpoint. Do not insert arbitrary small subdivisions, lift over an obstacle, or move directly across an obstacle to a later gap. Accept normal arrival error within 1 cm and move on instead of issuing a redundant correction to a reached endpoint.

If the expected endpoint has not been reached, retain the count and complete that leg. If localization is ambiguous, use the retained video's neighboring frames and the current wrist view to select the endpoint consistent with both route order and obstacle clearance; never choose a later occurrence merely because it is closer. If a direct recovery would intersect an obstacle, make a conservative planar correction toward the demonstrated safe corridor without advancing the count until its endpoint is reached. Do not issue an identical-pose motion. If all demonstrated legs are complete and the environment has not yet terminated, hold with a short wait solely to allow terminal evaluation; do not start an extra loop.

applied.refused: No memory fields or transitions change: all reported memory values were correct, and no additional unavailable historical fact was identified. No episode-specific coordinates, frame-to-endpoint lookup clauses, fixed offsets, nominal lengths, extra clearance, or motion subdivisions are added. Existing joint fitting, static-gap evidence pooling, final-tip corroboration, chronological repetition, and height rules remain rather than being duplicated. No earlier edit is reverted: worse aggregate scores alone do not establish that an earlier rule caused the errors, and this report supplies no such evidence. The changes strengthen physical-feature validation and cross-frame residual checking without claiming that sparse or occluded observations always determine endpoints within one centimetre.
